label: bm-hydrogels
topic: Printable hydrogels and swelling layers compatible with a desktop SLA printer
summary: Photocurable hydrogels DO print on desktop 405 nm vat printers, including a Formlabs machine. Burke 2020 printed PEGDMA-600 (TPO, 1 wt%) on a Formlabs Form 2 at 405 nm (gel fraction 97.6%); this CONTRADICTS the earlier claim in spec-resin-chemistry.json that no paper printed a hydrogel on a Formlabs printer. Measured swelling spans three orders of magnitude: stock-like neat PEGDA 250 swells 3.5% linear in 24 h, PEGDA 575+PEGMEMA 19.3%, PEGMEMA-based 74.1% (Maennel 2020, re-read); PEGDA 1.07/2.03/5.85 kDa swell to J=4.2-5.5 / 6.9-8.9 / 16.9-35.7 times dry volume (linear 1.6x-3.3x dry); GelMA 15% swells only 0.7-7.8% linear depending on exposure time; PNIPAm films deswell to 0.3-0.5 of area above LCST. The strongest new evidence for the project's bilayer law is a 405 nm LCD-printed GelMA bilayer whose bend is encoded purely by exposure time (linear swelling 7.83% at 30 s down to 0.70% at 70 s, E about 15-20 kPa): the Timoshenko ceiling (project record, f max = 1.5) predicts R = 10.9-11.0 mm for a 1 mm balanced strip against the paper's observed 11-20 mm range (my calculation; per-sample radii were in a figure I could not read). A new design consequence from the same formula: a soft hydrogel (about 20 kPa to 13 MPa) bonded to a stiff Formlabs resin (2.75-10 GPa) has f(m=1) of only 0.0000-0.11 and needs a hydrogel 15-725 times thicker than the stiff layer to reach the 1.5 ceiling, so the passive partner should be an elastomer (Silicone 40A / Flexible class) or the whole part should be a single hydrogel with a cure-depth gradient. Kinetics: a measured hydrogel cooperative diffusion constant of 8.8e-11 to 1.7e-10 m2/s gives tau = h^2/(pi^2 D) of 6-12 s at 0.1 mm and 10-19 min at 1 mm, i.e. a thin hydrogel layer equilibrates in minutes-to-hours, far faster than stock resins; but real printed gels were slower (24 h to equilibrate for 1.5 mm GelMA; about 2 weeks for a hydrophobically associated acrylic acid gel; 3-7.5 h to deswell a 0.5 mm PNIPAm film). Sensitive failure points found: oxygen inhibition (needs scavenger or oxygen-permeable window; PPh3 0.02-1 wt% used), under-cure and exposure-dependent swelling, residual photoinitiator/absorber (12 h ethanol wash needed for one PEGDA resin), hydrolytic ester loss of PEGDA, drying fracture, and very poor fatigue evidence (few actuators tested beyond 10 cycles). I also confirmed (from the Formlabs Flexible 80A V2 data sheet copy) the +8% mass / +3% volume in deionized water at 1 day that spec-formlabs-materials.json reported, and flag that it sits 10x above the 0.7% 24 h cube-test figure given for Flexible 80A in spec-resin-chemistry.json.
lay_summary: Some jelly-like plastics can be 3D printed with the same blue-violet light that Formlabs printers use. They are made mostly of water once they soak. When one face swells more than the other, a flat strip curls, like a drying leaf curling. In one experiment a printed jelly strip curled into a circle about 11 to 20 millimetres in radius just from being given different light doses on its two halves, which matches what our bending law predicts. The catch is that jelly is far softer than the hard resins Formlabs sells, so a jelly layer glued onto a hard layer barely bends, like trying to curl a plank by stretching a rubber band on it. A soft rubbery partner layer, or a jelly-only part, should work much better.

glossary.plain: a plastic network that soaks up a lot of water and swells like a sponge but keeps its shape
how much bigger or heavier a gel gets after soaking, compared with its dry size or weight
growth in length (not volume) after soaking, in percent
a liquid chemical (a polyethylene glycol with reactive ends) that turns into a water-loving gel when lit
gelatin (cooked collagen) chemically modified so light can set it into a gel
a gel that shrinks and turns cloudy when warmed above about 32 C and swells again when cooled
a chemical that absorbs light and starts the setting reaction (examples: LAP, TPO)
the blue-violet light colour used by Formlabs SLA printers
a paid Formlabs setting that lets you print with resins that are not Formlabs'
air in the liquid mops up the reaction so a thin layer near air or a window stays liquid or soft
stiffness: how hard you must push to bend or stretch a material
the formula for how much a two-layer strip curls when one layer grows more than the other
the share of the material that actually became part of the solid network instead of staying loose and washable
a number for how fast water moves into or out of a gel; time to soak scales as thickness squared divided by D
unreacted chemicals washing out of a printed part into water
the temperature above which a gel like PNIPAM squeezes its water out

findings.claim: A hydrogel (PEGDMA, Mw 600) was printed on a Formlabs Form 2 SLA printer at 405 nm; this contradicts spec-resin-chemistry.json, which found no paper printing a hydrogel on a Formlabs printer.
findings.value: Form 2, 250 mW laser, 405 nm, 50 um layers, 10 min Procure 350 post-cure
findings.evidence_quote: The 3D printing machine utilised was the Formlabs Form 2 SLA (Formlabs Inc., Somerville, MA, USA).

findings.claim: That Form 2 resin was neat PEGDMA with 1 wt% TPO as photoinitiator (the UV-chamber control used Irgacure 2959).
findings.evidence_quote: The mixtures were prepared pre-polymerisation by combining PEGDMA with either 1 wt% Irgacure 2959 photoinitiator or TPO.

findings.claim: Swelling ratio of the Form 2 printed PEGDMA gel in PBS was 41.7 versus 47.0 for UV-chamber cured; the text gives the number without units (the equation did not extract, so I cannot say if it is % or a ratio).
findings.evidence_quote: the swelling ratios of the UV chamber and SLA samples were shown to be significantly different at 47.0 and 41.7, respectively

findings.claim: Compressive Young's modulus of the Form 2 printed PEGDMA gel was 13.01 MPa versus 8.26 MPa for UV-chamber samples; tensile values were 15.47 and 19.92 MPa in the order the text lists (the text's ordering is ambiguous). Samples were stored in PBS at 37 C, hydration state at test not stated.
findings.value: compressive E 13.01 vs 8.26 MPa; tensile 15.47 / 19.92 MPa
findings.evidence_quote: with Young’s modulus values of 13.01 MPa and 8.26 MPa, respectively.

findings.claim: Gel fraction of the Form 2 printed gel was 97.58% (UV chamber 99.33%), i.e. 2.4% unreacted/extractable vs 0.67%, about four times more residue in the printed part; FTIR still showed a residual C=C peak.
findings.evidence_quote: results of 99.33% and 97.58% for the UV chamber and SLA samples, respectively.

findings.claim: A Formlabs user forum post shows a modified Form 1+ printing PEGDA with LAP and chlorophyll photoblocker; hydrogels do not stick to the aluminium build head, so silane-coated glass slides were used. No concentrations or exposures were given. (Fetched through a page summariser, so the quote is not independently verified.)
findings.value: PEGDA + LAP + chlorophyll; silane glass slide build surface
findings.evidence_quote: This allows hydrogels to stick on silane coated glass slide, since they won't stick to aluminium surface.

findings.claim: Re-read of Maennel 2020: printed 9 mm x 1 mm discs swell (diameter, PBS, 24 h) 3.5% for neat PEGDA 250, up to 19.3% for PEGDA+PEGMEMA blends, 74.1% for PEGMEMA-based, <0.5% for TPGDA; Asiga DLP at 385 nm, TPO 0.1% w/w and Sudan 1 absorber. Confirms the earlier agent's numbers.
findings.evidence_quote: By preparing mixtures of PEGDA and PEGMEMA (RC1 to RC4), we drastically reduced the swelling ratio varying from 3.5% (RC1) up to 19.3% (RC4).

findings.claim: PEGDA swelling rises steeply with molecular weight. Measured volumetric swelling J (swollen/dry volume) of LAP-cured PEGDA discs: 4.2-5.5 at Mn 1.07 kDa, 6.9-8.9 at 2.03 kDa, 16.9-35.7 at 5.85 kDa, the range spanning as-cured concentrations 25.7-17.9, 21.0-15.8 and 15.9-8.0 wt%. My conversion to linear size vs dry: 1.6-1.8x, 1.9-2.1x, 2.6-3.3x.
findings.source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11325651/ Table 2 (Macromolecules 2024, doi 10.1021/acs.macromol.3c02635); conversion in scripts/bm-hydrogels/calcs.py section 1

findings.claim: Lower PEGDA molecular weight and higher concentration raise modulus and lower swelling (GelMA/PEGDA hybrid bioinks with PEGDA Mn 700, 2000, 4000; compressive moduli 50 kPa for 10% GelMA to 600 kPa for the 15% PEGDA-700 hybrid). Extrusion printing at 405 nm, not vat printing.
findings.evidence_quote: A lower molecular weight and high concentration induced high crosslinking density thus improving compressive modulus, lower swelling, and a slower degradation profile.

findings.claim: In frontal-photopolymerised asymmetric PEGDA networks (Mn 250, 575, 700; Irgacure-819), the higher-Mn network swells more, tied to a larger mesh size. Numbers are in supplementary figures I did not read.
findings.evidence_quote: The high-Mn polymer network is capable of absorbing more solvent and undergoing greater swelling (see Figures S5 and S6), which we associate to its larger network mesh size.

findings.claim: LAP absorbs 365 nm strongly (epsilon 218 M-1 cm-1) and also gels PEGDA at 405 nm (2.2 mM, 10 mW/cm2: 120 s gel time) whereas Irgacure 2959 did not gel in 1800 s at 405 nm. Water solubility of LAP is far better than TPO's, which is why LAP is the hydrogel photoinitiator of choice at 405 nm.
findings.value: epsilon(365)=218 M-1cm-1; gel time 120 s at 405 nm, 10 mW/cm2, 2.2 mM

findings.claim: GelMA compressive modulus is only a few to about 30 kPa: 2.0, 10.0, 22.0 kPa for 5, 10, 15% w/v at 53.8% methacrylation, and 3.3, 16.0, 30.0 kPa at 81.4% (a review restating Nichol 2010). Mass swelling ratio falls with higher concentration and methacrylation (numbers only in Nichol's figure).
findings.evidence_quote: Nichol et al. estimated compressive modulus values of 2.0, 10.0, and 22.0 KPa, respectively, for 5, 10, and 15% w/v GelMA (with a degree of substitution of 53.8%).

findings.claim: GelMA was printed on a consumer 405 nm LCD printer (Frozen Sonic Mini 8K, 1.4 mW/cm2) at 50 um layers with 20-70 s exposure per layer, using 15% w/v GelMA, 1% w/v LAP and 1.5 mM tartrazine absorber. Per-layer exposure is orders of magnitude longer than the 550 ms used for PEGDA with a strong absorber on a custom 385 nm printer (Warr 2020).
findings.value: 1.4 mW/cm2; 20-70 s per 50 um layer; 15 % GelMA, 1 % LAP, 1.5 mM tartrazine
findings.evidence_quote: Printability was evaluated using a Frozen Sonic Mini 8K LCD printer (405 nm, 1.4 mW/cm2 light intensity

findings.claim: In that GelMA print, 24 h linear swelling in culture medium fell monotonically with exposure time: 7.83% (30 s), 7.11% (40 s), 5.52% (50 s), 2.02% (60 s), 0.70% (70 s); modulus rose 14.48 -> 20.23 kPa; gel fraction 70.4 -> 80.7%. So exposure time alone gives about 7 percentage points of differential linear strain.

Two-region GelMA strips (20 x 2 x 1 mm, 35 s and 65 s halves) bent on swelling to radii of curvature between 11 and 20 mm depending on geometry; balanced thickness splits curved most; finite-element simulation matched. Direct vat-printed precedent for a swelling bilayer.
findings.value: R = 11-20 mm (per-sample values in Fig 5a not read)
findings.evidence_quote: enabling controlled bending of the printed structures upon immersion in aqueous media, with radii of curvature between 11 and 20 mm depending on the geometry.

findings.claim: OWN CALCULATION: applying the project-record Timoshenko coefficient to the GelMA numbers (active layer 35 s, LS 7.47%, E 14.9 kPa; passive 65 s, LS 1.36%, E 19.4 kPa; d_eps 0.0611, n 0.766, h 1 mm) gives f = 1.493 at m=1 and kappa 0.0912 1/mm, R = 11.0 mm; ceiling R = 10.9 mm. The observed minimum of the quoted range, 11 mm, is consistent with the law; the 11-20 mm spread says unbalanced layers fall short. Caveat: interpolated table values and an unread per-sample figure.
findings.source: scripts/bm-hydrogels/calcs.py section 2, output in scratch/bm-hydrogels/calcs_output.txt; project record for f(m,n)

findings.claim: OWN CALCULATION, design consequence: because the optimum m* = n^-1/2 requires the soft layer to be thicker, a hydrogel on a stiff Formlabs resin is mechanically dead. GelMA (about 19 kPa) on Grey/Clear V5 (2.75 GPa): f(m=1)=0.0002, m*=380; on Rigid 10K (10 GPa): f(m=1)=0.00005, m*=725; PEGDMA-600 (13 MPa) on Clear V5: f(m=1)=0.11, m*=14.5. Against a 0.2 mm Form 4 minimum wall this needs 76 mm of GelMA. With soft elastomer partners (my secant estimates from spec-formlabs-materials.json): GelMA on Silicone 40A m*=6.5, f(1)=0.43; PEGDMA-600 on Silicone 40A m*=0.25; on Flexible 80A V2 m*=0.67, f(1)=1.44. This does not contradict the 'modulus drops out' result; it says the thickness ratio that makes it drop out is impractical for a large modulus gap.
findings.source: scripts/bm-hydrogels/calcs.py section 9; moduli from spec-formlabs-materials.json, spec-resin-chemistry.json and PMC13205297, PMC7564751

findings.claim: Poly(acrylamide) 'tanglemer' hydrogels made with LAP and DLP-printed (same paper benchmarks Formlabs Silicone 40A and Elastic 50A) swell to a ratio of about 4 (about 80 wt% water), with tensile modulus under 100 kPa (143 to 66 kPa as initiator drops from 0.01 to 0.0001 mol%). The soft, tough network needs very low initiator, i.e. slow exposures (30-60 s per 100 um layer for the elastomer case).
findings.value: swelling ratio ~4; 80 wt% H2O; E_T 66-143 kPa
findings.evidence_quote: At equilibrium, all LAP‐derived hydrogels exhibited swelling ratios of ∼4, corresponding to ≈ 80 wt% H2O (Table S34, Equation S6).

findings.claim: Acrylic acid / hexadecyl acrylate copolymer gels (2 wt% TPO, Creality Halot-one, 405 nm cure) have equilibrium water content of 51% falling to 7% as the hydrophobic fraction rises, and took about 2 weeks to equilibrate; tensile Young's modulus 23-215 MPa (test state not stated). My conversion: EWC 51% is a 2.04x mass ratio, about 27% linear; 7% is about 2% linear.
findings.evidence_quote: The equilibrium water content (EWC) of the printed hydrogels was determined by keeping the hydrogel specimen in water until obtaining the swelling equilibrium, which required about 2 weeks.

findings.claim: PNIPAm hydrogel films cured on an Anycubic Photon D2 (405 nm, 2.5 mW/cm2) with PEGDA-700 plus BIS crosslinkers and a BAPO-type initiator in acetone-water: areal deswelling above the LCST (35 C) was 0.3-0.5 of the as-printed area (linear 0.55-0.71, my conversion); 50 s vs 120 s exposure gave modulus 40.2 vs 123.2 kPa. Heating through the LCST took 7.5 h (3 h with accelerated heating) to reveal a halftone image in a film printed in a 450-550 um cell.
findings.evidence_quote: The 50-s hydrogel film had a Young’s modulus of 40.23 kPa and a strain at a break of 1102%, whereas the 120-s film exhibited a Young’s modulus of 123.24 kPa

findings.claim: Measured cooperative-diffusion swelling constants for a hydrogel (polyampholyte gel, 1.1-1.3 mm thick) are 8.8e-11 to 1.7e-10 m2/s, with swelling time proportional to thickness squared via tau = h^2/(pi^2 D). Not PEGDA or GelMA; transfers as an order of magnitude only.
findings.evidence_quote: The cooperative diffusion coefficient of swelling, Dsw, increases slightly from 8.8 × 10−11 to 1.7 × 10−10 m2/s by increasing CMBAA from 0 to 5.0 mol% (Fig. 4A).

findings.claim: OWN CALCULATION: with D = 8.8e-11 to 1.7e-10 m2/s, tau = h^2/(pi^2 D) is 6-12 s at 0.1 mm, 2.5-4.8 min at 0.5 mm, 10-19 min at 1 mm and 40-77 min at 2 mm; five tau (near equilibrium) is 0.8-1.6 h at 1 mm. Printed gels were slower than this estimate (24 h chosen for 1.5 mm GelMA; 3-7.5 h PNIPAm film; 2 weeks for the hydrophobic AAc gel), so measure D on the real resin.
findings.value: tau 6-12 s (0.1 mm) to 40-77 min (2 mm)

findings.claim: Review of hydrogel actuators: bilayer bending angles span 20-720 degrees with actuation times 1-280 min; no clear relation between bending angle and bilayer thickness or modulus; bending follows the strain difference between layers, as the Timoshenko beam equation says. Actuation time grew from 1 min to 5 min when a 450-degree bilayer thickness was doubled to 2 mm.
findings.evidence_quote: The bending angle of bilayer actuators can range from 20 to 720° with actuation times varying from 1 to 280 min (Fig. 2a).

findings.claim: Hydrogel actuator forces are small: single-network hydrogels have kPa to hundreds of kPa modulus, so swelling and contraction forces are mostly below 1 N, about an order of magnitude below pine-cone scales (about 10 N).
findings.evidence_quote: the swelling and contraction forces for most hydrogel actuators are less than 1 N,8,42 even though the osmotic pressure that drives swelling can reach megapascals.

findings.claim: Fatigue is the least-tested failure point: few hydrogel actuators are cycled beyond 10 times and drying during a fatigue test confounds the result; stiffer hydrogels tend to be less fatigue resistant.
findings.value: repeatable actuation beyond 10 cycles rarely shown
findings.evidence_quote: Indeed, few studies demonstrate repeatable actuation beyond 10 cycles, and even fewer conduct long-term fatigue testing.

findings.claim: Oxygen inhibition is a design lever and a failure point: an oxygen-permeable window creates a persistent liquid 'dead zone' in CLIP, and oxygen inhibition worsens as feature size shrinks in PEGDA. A DLP tanglemer study adds 0.02-1 wt% triphenylphosphine to mitigate it.
findings.evidence_quote: To accelerate photopolymerization and mitigate oxygen inhibition, triphenylphosphine (PPh3, 0.02–1 wt%) was added to the EA resins

findings.claim: Incomplete or graded cure changes swelling and leaves porosity: PEGDA micro-stereolithography shows a graded degree of cure, submicron pores and irreversible densification depending on exposure time and intensity. In the GelMA print, 30 vs 70 s exposure changed gel fraction 70% to 81%.
findings.source: doi 10.1039/d1sm00483b (Alketbi 2021, abstract via Europe PMC PMID 34269366); https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13205297/
findings.evidence_quote: Our findings show that the degree of curing exhibits a graded profile from confocal Raman spectroscopy and submicron pores from atomic force microscopy

findings.claim: Leaching: a custom PEGDA resin with a UV absorber (2-nitrophenyl phenyl sulfide) needed a 12 h ethanol wash to be non-cytotoxic; an avobenzone-absorber variant was non-cytotoxic as printed. Any photoinitiator/absorber not bound into the network is a leachable.
findings.evidence_quote: We show that NPS-PEGDA can be made effectively non-cytotoxic with a post-print 12-hour ethanol wash, and that A-PEGDA, as-printed, is effectively non-cytotoxic.

findings.claim: Printed soft networks can leave 5-23% sol: DLP-printed elastomer tanglemers rose from 77-87% to 91-95% gel fraction with a 10 min 365 nm post-cure, and omitting UV post-cure left a roughly 5% volume decrease on drying.
findings.evidence_quote: post‐curing with 5 mW cm− 2 365 nm light for 10 min before drying increased gel fractions from 77% to 91% and from 87% to 95%

findings.claim: Hydrolysis: PEGDA gels degrade by ester hydrolysis, seen as rising swelling ratio and falling modulus; 10 kDa PEGDA 10 wt% gels degraded significantly in 12 weeks in vivo, whereas the amide analogue did not. A PEGDA active layer will drift to larger swelling over weeks.
findings.evidence_quote: PEGDAA hydrogels remained stable over 12 weeks of subcutaneous implantation in a rat model while PEGDA hydrogels underwent significant degradation as indicated by both increased swelling ratio and decreased modulus.

findings.claim: Dehydration cracking: drying produces fracture by local dehydration of a brittle PEGDA gel (shown in freezing); partially dried gels behave as incompressible solids with environment-set target volumes. I found no measured critical thickness or drying rate for a printed hydrogel. Peer-reviewed numbers for printed gels were not found; APS abstracts seen in a search snippet (volatile solvents crack more, thickness and crosslinker density matter little) were not read.
findings.source: arXiv:2401.12871 (Yang et al., export API) ; arXiv:2606.07384 (Chao Correas et al.)
findings.evidence_quote: Instead, local ice growth dehydrates the surrounding hydrogel, leading to drying-induced fracture.

findings.claim: Hydrogel to printed substrate: a silane (TMSPMA) anchored tough hydrogel gave interfacial toughness over 1000 J/m2; a non-tough PAAm gel was limited to 24 J/m2 by its own fracture toughness, and without anchoring only 8 J/m2. A cast hydrogel on a printed resin needs covalent anchoring, not just contact.
findings.evidence_quote: Here, we report a design strategy and a set of simple fabrication methods to give extremely tough and functional bonding between hydrogels and diverse solids

findings.claim: Multi-material on a single-vat desktop SLA printer is possible by pausing, swapping resin and cleaning ('Print-Pause-Print'); acrylate-rich interfaces between PEGDA variants bonded strongly and did not delaminate. Printer was a desktop DLP, not a Formlabs. PEGDA 258 Mw printed modulus about 870 MPa; adding PEGMEMA brought it to about 2.2 MPa; solvent/water uptake of the blends below 8% mass and 10% volume.
findings.source: arXiv:2305.14190 (Ahmadianyazdi, Miller, Folch 2023; PDF read locally)
findings.evidence_quote: the abundance of unsaturated acrylate groups at these interfaces led to a strong adhesion between different polymers and prevented delamination.

findings.claim: Contradiction check: the Formlabs Flexible 80A V2 data sheet (copy dated 12/05/2026) lists deionized water at 1 day: -26 Shore A, +8% mass, +3% volume; 1 week +9% mass, +7% volume. This confirms spec-formlabs-materials.json and sits about 10x above the 0.7% 24 h cube figure for Flexible 80A in spec-resin-chemistry.json. The TDS copy I read had the cube table text missing, so I could not settle the 0.7%; the methods differ (ASTM D471 slabs vs 1 cm cubes).

Macroporous (emulsion) GelMA printed on an Anycubic Photon Mono SE (405 nm, 1.68 mW/cm2) swells to 2524% (DI) and 2261% (PBS) of its mass after 72 h; this shows swelling in printed gels can be raised by porosity but compressive modulus there was only 0.34 kPa.
findings.evidence_quote: Group 3 exhibited the highest swelling ratios after 72 h in both deionized water (2524%) and PBS buffer (2261%)

findings.claim: Swelling and stiffness trade off: raising swelling ratio from about 200% to about 800% gives a two- to four-fold fall in Young's modulus (review). Relevant because the active layer softens as it swells.
findings.evidence_quote: hydrogels with swelling ratios increasing from ~200% to ~800% can exhibit a two- to four-fold decrease in Young’s modulus

findings.claim: HEMA: no measured swelling or modulus for a vat-printed pHEMA gel was found. The only vat-printable HEMA hit was a PHEMA-polysilsesquioxane resin (abstract only): more silsesquioxane reduced swelling and hydration markedly decreased compressive resistance.
findings.source: doi 10.1039/d6tb00727a (J. Mater. Chem. B 2026, abstract via Europe PMC PMID 42596689)
findings.evidence_quote: Increasing PSS content reduced swelling, while TEGDMA produced more rigid networks than PEGDMA. Hydration markedly decreased compressive resistance

key_claims.claim: A PEGDMA-600 hydrogel (1 wt% TPO) has been printed on a Formlabs Form 2 at 405 nm with 97.6% gel fraction, so hydrogel printing on a Formlabs printer has a published precedent (contradicting the earlier agent).
key_claims.evidence_quote: The 3D printing machine utilised was the Formlabs Form 2 SLA (Formlabs Inc., Somerville, MA, USA).

key_claims.claim: A 405 nm LCD-printed GelMA strip programmed only by per-layer exposure (linear swelling 7.83% at 30 s to 0.70% at 70 s, E about 15-20 kPa) bent to radii of 11-20 mm; the project Timoshenko ceiling predicts about 11 mm for a balanced 1 mm strip.
key_claims.evidence_quote: enabling controlled bending of the printed structures upon immersion in aqueous media, with radii of curvature between 11 and 20 mm depending on the geometry.

key_claims.claim: Printed PEG-acrylate swelling is tunable over about 0.5% to 74% linear in 24 h by monomer choice (Maennel), and PEGDA volumetric swelling rises from J about 4-5 at 1 kDa to about 17-36 at 5.85 kDa.
key_claims.evidence_quote: Finally, TPGDA-based resins showed the lowest swelling ratio with less than 0.5% over a period of 24 h in PBS.

key_claims.claim: By the project's own f(m,n), a kPa-to-MPa hydrogel on a GPa Formlabs resin needs a hydrogel 15-725 times thicker than the stiff layer to reach the 1.5 ceiling (my calculation), so the passive layer should be an elastomer or the part a single graded hydrogel.
key_claims.source: scripts/bm-hydrogels/calcs.py section 9 (inputs: PMC13205297 Table 1; PMC7564751; spec-formlabs-materials.json)

recommendations: Do not pair a thin kPa-MPa hydrogel layer with Rigid 10K, Clear/Grey V5 or other GPa resins: by the project's f(m,n) the hydrogel must be 15-725 times thicker than the stiff layer, which is not printable at the 0.2 mm minimum wall. Choose a soft passive partner (Silicone 40A / Flexible 80A class) or a hydrogel-only part with a through-thickness cure gradient.

First proof of concept: Form 4 Open Material Mode, neat PEGDMA-600 or PEGDA-575 plus PEGMEMA with TPO (Burke recipe is the only Formlabs precedent), coupons of three thicknesses (0.2, 0.5, 1.0 mm), measure linear swelling versus time in water, E wet and dry, and gel fraction. This replaces the unknown D and hygroscopic strain with measured values.

Alternative with much stronger precedent for bending: GelMA (or PEGDA) with a UV absorber printed with two exposure doses per layer, since exposure time alone moved linear swelling from 7.8% to 0.7% and produced R = 11-20 mm. Needs a long per-layer exposure on a 405 nm LCD (20-70 s), so test whether Form 4 can reach those doses in the Print Settings Editor.

Plan for oxygen inhibition (scavenger such as 0.1 wt% triphenylphosphine, nitrogen, or an oxygen-permeable interface), leachables (extended ethanol or water wash and a gel-fraction check), hydrolysis drift (avoid PEGDA over months or use methacrylamide variants), and slow drying (keep hydrated or use a glycerol or humectant solvent).

Open questions to resolve before a purchase: whether a water-based hydrogel resin damages the Form 4 resin tank film or cartridge seals, and whether the printer can pause for resin exchange (Print-Pause-Print). I found no source on either.

could_not_find: Equilibrium swelling and wet modulus for any hydrogel printed on a Form 3 or Form 4 (the only Formlabs print is Form 2 PEGDMA; Form 3 appears in other papers only as the maker of mould or spacer parts). The definition and units of Burke's 'swelling ratio' 41.7 did not extract.

Any peer-reviewed measurement of a HEMA/pHEMA vat-printed gel's swelling ratio, equilibrium water content or modulus. The pHEMA equilibrium water content of roughly 40% from contact-lens literature is unverified background and I did not use it.
A measured water diffusivity or time to equilibrium for printed PEGDA or GelMA layers at 0.1-1 mm: the only measured D is for a polyampholyte gel, so tau figures are order-of-magnitude.
Per-sample bending radii of the GelMA bilayer (only the 11-20 mm range is in text; per-sample values are in Fig. 5a), so my 11 mm prediction cannot be compared sample by sample.
Hydrogel fatigue numbers for printed PEG or GelMA actuators (cycles to failure, threshold toughness): the review says few studies go beyond 10 cycles.
Drying-crack thresholds (critical thickness, humidity, rate) for printed hydrogels; only the arXiv mechanism papers and APS meeting abstracts (seen as search snippets, not opened) were found.
Numerical swelling for PEGDA/PPGDMA (Zhao 2018) and the polyurethane/sodium acrylate cuff (Hiendlmeier 2023): full texts paywalled, as in the earlier agents.
Whether a water-based hydrogel resin is safe for the Form 4 resin tank film, cartridge or wiper, and whether Form 4 can pause mid-print for resin exchange; Open Material Mode price. No source found.
Quantitative leachable (TPO, LAP, absorber) amounts from printed hydrogels into water; only a wash-time result for one resin (Warr 2020).

A Springer paper (J. Mater. Res., doi 10.1557/s43578-021-00411-2) that a search linked to PEGDA on a Form 2 could not be opened (access redirect), so I did not use it; an acrylamide/PEGDA700 + cellulose nanocrystal Form 2 paper named in a search snippet was not located in Europe PMC.
Primary figures for Nichol 2010 (moduli and swelling are in figures); I used Yue 2015's restatement of them.

My use of the Timoshenko formula assumes small-strain linear elasticity and a swollen modulus; hydrogels at 7% to 70% strain and with time-varying modulus violate this, and no measurement of f for hydrogels on stiff resins exists.
